Nāgarakhaṇḍa
------------------------------------------
This is a section of the Skandapurāṇa wherein the stories of हरिश्चन्द्र, Viśvā-मित्र and the manifestation of शिवलिङ्ग are described. See SKANDAPURĀṆA for more details.

nāgara
------------------------------------------
Nāgara is one of the three styles of temple architecture, the other two being वेसर and द्राविड.
In this type, which is more common to North India, the plan is square and the towers are curvilinear.
See also HINDU TEMPLES.

Nāgoji Bhaṭṭa
------------------------------------------
Nāgoji भट्ट (also called Nāgeśa भट्ट) lived in the early part of the 18th century. He was the son of शिव भट्ट and सती. The famous Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita (author of the monumental work on Sanskrit grammar, the Siddhānta Kaumudī) was his grandfather. A ब्राह्मण from Maharashtra, he lived mostly at Śṛṅgaverapura near Allahabad, as a protege of a chieftain, राम of the Bisena family.
His great erudition has been reflected in his various writings, profuse in quantity and excellent in quality. Apart from grammar and poetics he was also an expert in the field of धर्मशास्त्रस्.
Some of his works are: several treatises ending with the word ‘induśekhara’ such as Ācārenduśekhara, Tīrthendu-śekhara, Prāyaścittenduśekhara and so on, on the dharmaśāstra subjects; commen-taries on the Kuvalayānanda, Rasagaṅgādhara and other treatises on poetics; Paribhāṣenduśekhara on grammar and many other books.

nāgavāyu
(‘the air or प्राण that does not move’)
------------------------------------------
Life and health of the human body are maintained by the पञ्चप्राणस् or the five vital airs. नागवायु, also called नाग, is an upaprāṇa, a minor प्राण, considered as an aspect of उदान. It is responsible for bringing about eructation and vomiting.
See also PAÑCAPRĀṆAS.

Nāgapañcamī
(‘the fifth day sacred to नाग or the Snake-deity’)
------------------------------------------
Nāgapañcamī (śrāvaṇa-śukla-pañcamī) is an important festival, observed as a vrata with religious vows in many parts of India.
Serpent worship seems to be a very ancient phenomenon in India. Fear of death due to serpent-bite, especially in the rainy season, may have been the origin of the नागपञ्चमी, in which worship of serpents—especially the cobra—is the main act. On this day, considered to be as auspicious as the Akṣayyatṛtīyā, bathing the mythical serpents—Vāsuki, तक्षक, Kāliya, Maṇibhadra, ऐरावत, Dhṛta-rāṣṭra, Kārkotaka and Dhanañjaya—with milk through images, is supposed to give abhaya or freedom from dangers, especially from snakebite. Figures of snakes are drawn on the walls on either side of the main entrance door, with cowdung, and worship is offered to them. The same may be done to figures of snakes drawn with red sandal paste on wooden boards also. Images used in worship for bathing may be made of metal or clay. Worship should include करवीर flowers, incense and the ड़ोओद् offering of pāyasa (pudding). Inviting the snake-charmers and feeding their snakes with milk is common on this day.
In Bengal, Manasādevī (a snake-goddess) is worshipped on Śrāvaṇa कृष्ण pañcamī, in one’s own courtyard. The general purpose and procedure of worship are the same. Keeping the neem leaves in the होउसे and eating a few of them at the end is the only speciality.

nāgapāśa
(‘serpent rope’)
------------------------------------------
As a weapon of war, नागपाश is that arrow which becomes a snake and binds the enemy. It was used by इन्द्रजित् (Rāvaṇa’s son) against राम and लक्ष्मण (vide Rāmāyaṇa 6.45).
Nāgapāśa, in iconographical works, is shown as a coiled serpent (with two and a half coils) in the hands of certain deities like दुर्गा. When it is thrown against an enemy, he can never escape from it.

Nāga
(‘that which exists in mountains,’ ‘that which burns [us with its poison],’ ‘snake or serpent’)
------------------------------------------
Snake-worship seems to be a very ancient custom. Images of snake-couples have been unearthed in the इन्दुस् वल्लेय् चिविलिसतिओन्. Worship of snakes is said to have existed in ancient Greece, Egypt and Assyria.
अश्वत्थ tree">Nāga Serpents under अश्वत्थ treeAccording to the पुराणस्, snakes (serpent-gods) are the offsprings of the sage कश्यप and his wife कद्रू. Names of the famous great serpents which were their original progeny are: अनन्त (or शेष), वासुकि, तक्षक, Kārkoṭaka, पद्म, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, Dhanañjaya and Kulika.
Snakes and serpents find an important place in our mythological literature. If विष्णु is comfortably reclining on it in the ocean of milk, शिव wears it all over his body as ornaments! If गणपति wears it as यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread) and uses another as his belt to keep his belly in position, his brother सुब्रह्मण्य considers it as his another form.
The works on योग compare the कुण्डलिनी power to a coiled serpent.
Snakes are worshipped for obtaining wealth and children, for long-life and for escaping from snake-bites.
Establishing relief figures of snakes, especially under the अश्वत्थ trees (Ficus religiosa), is considered as a sacred act bringing religious merit. Killing of snakes, that too of cobras, is considered as heinous and sinful. Dead snakes are cremated with religious honours.
Nāgas or snakes are a familiar motif in temple sculpture.
Elaborate rituals connected with Nāgamaṇḍalas, where complicated designs are drawn and worshipped, are found in certain parts of India, especially in the west-coastal region of South.
Sarpabali or offerings to snakes involving elaborate rituals, songs and dances, is a speciality in the Kerala State of South India.
Nāgapañcamī is a famous festival connected with स्नके-wओर्स्हिप्.
(See NĀGAPAÑCAMĪ for details.)
The word denotes an elephant also.
The नागस् were a particular race of people, probably with the snake banner, referred to in the Mahābhārata. Historically also, there were नाग rulers in Madhya Pradesh and Kashmir.

Nāgas
------------------------------------------
One of the wives of अर्जुन, the Pāṇḍava hero, was Ulūpī, a नाग princess. Obviously, the नागस् must have been a prominent race of human beings. They might have derived their name either because they were worshippers of snake-gods or had the snake as their national symbol.
The पुराणस् describe them as the offsprings of the sage कश्यप and his wife कद्रू and often identified with snakes.
Nāga tribal in his traditional attireThe नागस् of the mythical period lived in the subterranean world called रसातल. Their capital was Bhogavatī, a beautiful city.
During the historical period, two royal families of नागस् have been known to exist. They are: the Chindakas who ruled from Cakrakoṭṭa (Bastar of Madhya Pradesh) (11th to 14th century A. D.); the Sindas of Karnataka (circa A. D. 750), who called their land as Sindavāḍi.
The नागस् of modern India are a group of tribals inhabiting the नाग Hill ranges of Nagaland in the north-east. They include more than 20 tribes of mixed origin and varying cultures. They differ in physical appearance too. Their dialects belong to the Sino-Tibetan group of languages. English, Hindī or broken Assamese is the common language for all.
The largest tribes are the Konyak, Ao, Tanghkul, Sema and Angami.
Most of them live in small villages placed on hill-sides and located near water.
Rice and millets are the staple ड़ोओद्. Weaving and wood-carving are the main sources of income.
A tribal council of elders rules over the tribes.
A sizeable section of the नागस् are christians.
As regards the नाग-साधुस्, see under MONASTICISM.

Nāgārjuna
------------------------------------------
Two Nāgārjunas are known to history though, sometimes, they are considered as one and the same person.
The first नागार्जुन might have existed during the period 1st century B. C. to 1st century A. D. (15 B. C.—A. D. 75). Born into a ब्राह्मण family, he got converted to बुद्धिस्म्, by Aśvaghoṣa or Saraha. He was first known as Prajñādhara and later as नागार्जुन. He was the founder of the Mādhyamika school of बुद्धिस्म्. He wrote the Mādhyamika Kārikā as the basic work of this school. The place where he lived with his disciples and died is the नागार्जुन Koṇḍa area of Andhra Pradesh in the district of Guntur. It is now submerged under the water of नागार्जुन Sāgara.
The second नागार्जुन lived in the 6th century A. D. and belonged to the Karnataka State. He was the son of one Pādaliptasūri and a great scholar of जैनिस्म्, Vedānta and आयुर्वेद. He later on embraced बुद्धिस्म् and was the head of a monastery in Tibet for a few years.
He was an expert in रसविद्या (a branch of आयुर्वेद, using mercury as the main ingredient of medicines).
Later in life he settled down in श्रीशैलम् of Andhra Pradesh where he perfected his रसविद्या. His works on this science are: Rasakacchapuṭa and Kakṣa-puṭatantra (or Siddhacāmuṇḍa).
